cards.q: What is the embryological origin and classification of the mammary gland?
cards.a: It is a modified sweat gland derived from specialized ectoderm, functioning physiologically as an exocrine gland with an arborizing ductal drainage system.

cards.q: At what gestational age do primitive mammary tissues and milk lines first develop?
cards.a: Primitive mammary tissue is detectable by the 6th gestational week as bilateral ectodermal thickenings (milk lines) extending from the axillae to the groins.

cards.q: Which anatomical portion of the embryonic milk line normally persists in humans?
cards.a: Only the middle part of the upper 1/3 of each mammary ridge persists, while cranial and caudal remnants undergo physiological apoptosis and regress.

cards.q: What congenital anomalies arise from the failure of embryonic milk line regression?
cards.a: Supernumerary nipples (polythelia) or accessory mammary tissue/breasts (polymazia) along the anatomical milk line.

cards.q: What is polythelia and what common dermatologic entity can it mimic?
cards.a: The presence of accessory (supernumerary) nipples along the milk line; it is frequently mistaken clinically for melanocytic nevi (moles).

cards.q: What are the clinical differences and significance between congenital and acquired nipple inversion?
cards.a:
• Congenital: Typically bilateral, present since childhood, caused by mesenchymal proliferation failure or short lactiferous ducts.
• Acquired: Recent or unilateral retraction in an adult, which is a major red flag for invasive carcinoma (due to desmoplastic cicatricial traction).

cards.q: What is Poland syndrome and which specific muscle head is congenitally absent?
cards.a: Congenital unilateral absence of breast tissue (amazia) associated with absence of the sternocostal head of the pectoralis major (the clavicular head is spared and latissimus dorsi is intact).

cards.q: What associated defects occur in Poland syndrome besides pectoral muscle and breast absence?
cards.a: Ipsilateral chest wall hypoplasia, absence of ribs 2–4, and upper extremity syndactyly or brachydactyly.

cards.q: Why does polymazia (supernumerary breast) undergo enlargement during pregnancy and lactation?
cards.a: Because it contains true hormone-sensitive glandular epithelium that responds to pregnancy hormones and puerperal lactational signals.

cards.q: In which anatomical fascial plane does the breast lie, and what is the sole exception?
cards.a: It lies entirely within the superficial fascia of the anterior chest wall, except for the axillary tail of Spence, which pierces the deep axillary fascia.

cards.q: Through which anatomical opening does the axillary tail of Spence pierce the deep fascia?
cards.a: The foramen of Langer, placing it into direct contact with axillary neurovascular structures and lymph nodes.

cards.q: What is the surgical significance of the retromammary space?
cards.a: It is a loose areolar cleft separating the deep surface of the breast from the deep pectoral fascia, allowing free mobility of the gland over the underlying chest wall.

cards.q: What are the true horizontal and vertical anatomical boundaries of the female breast?
cards.a:
• Vertical: 2nd rib down to the 6th rib.
• Horizontal: Lateral sternal border medially to the midaxillary line laterally (does not reach the posterior axillary line).

cards.q: What are the microscopic glandular extension limits of the breast that dictate wide flaps during mastectomy?
cards.a:
• Superiorly: Clavicle
• Inferiorly: Rectus sheath
• Medially: Sternal midline
• Laterally: Anterior border of latissimus dorsi

cards.q: What constitutes the functional and histopathological unit of the breast?
cards.a: The Terminal Ductal Lobular Unit (TDLU), which is the target of ovarian hormones and the site of origin for >90% of breast diseases (fibroadenomas, cysts, ductal/lobular carcinomas).

cards.q: What are the suspensory ligaments of Cooper and what causes senescent breast ptosis?
cards.a: Fibrous fascial bands running from the deep pectoral fascia to the dermis; loss of collagen/elastin within these ligaments alongside glandular atrophy leads to breast ptosis (corrected via mastopexy).

cards.q: What is the primary arterial blood supply to the breast and how much volume does it provide?
cards.a: The Internal Mammary Artery (Internal Thoracic Artery), supplying 50%–60% of total mammary blood flow via anterior perforating branches through the 2nd, 3rd, and 4th intercostal spaces.

cards.q: Which artery supplies the lateral quadrants of the breast and lateral thoracic wall?
cards.a: The Lateral Thoracic Artery, which originates from the second part of the axillary artery.

cards.q: What vascular anatomical mechanism explains early vertebral and pelvic metastases from breast cancer without pulmonary involvement?
cards.a: Direct, valveless communications between the posterior intercostal veins and the internal vertebral venous plexus of Batson.

cards.q: What percentage of mammary lymphatic drainage flows to the axillary lymph nodes versus the internal mammary nodes?
cards.a:
• Axillary nodes: ~75% (primary route of cancer dissemination)
• Internal mammary nodes: ~20% (drains primarily the medial quadrants)

cards.q: What anatomical muscle defines the three Berg surgical levels of axillary lymph nodes?
cards.a: The Pectoralis Minor muscle (never the pectoralis major).

cards.q: What are the anatomical definitions of Berg axillary node Levels I, II, and III?
cards.a:
• Level I: Lateral to the lateral border of pectoralis minor (pectoral, subscapular, and axillary vein groups).
• Level II: Behind/deep to pectoralis minor (central group and Rotter's interpectoral nodes).
• Level III: Medial to the medial border of pectoralis minor (apical/subclavicular nodes).

cards.q: What is the single most common and urgent presenting symptom of breast pathology?
cards.a: A palpable breast mass (demands immediate workup to definitively exclude malignancy).

cards.q: Why is an isolated nipple discharge without a lump statistically reassuring?
cards.a: Isolated discharge is overwhelmingly due to benign causes (intraductal papilloma, duct ectasia, inflammation); primary invasive carcinoma rarely presents with isolated discharge without a palpable mass.

cards.q: What is the initial radiological investigation of choice for a breast mass in a woman < 35 years versus ≥ 35–40 years?
cards.a:
• < 35 years: Breast Ultrasound (sonomammography), due to dense radiopaque glandular parenchyma.
• ≥ 35–40 years: Mammography, due to progressive replacement of radiodense glandular tissue with radiolucent fat.

cards.q: What clinical features characterize a classic hard fibroadenoma?
cards.a: Occurs in women aged 16–25 years, rubbery firm, small (< 5 cm), smooth, and highly encapsulated/hypermobile ('breast mouse').

cards.q: How does a soft fibroadenoma differ from a hard fibroadenoma regarding age, size, and consistency?
cards.a: Presents in premenopausal women aged 30–40 years, is soft, larger (> 5 cm), lobulated, and less mobile due to increased cellularity/myxoid stroma.

cards.q: What are the distinguishing clinical and metastatic features of Cystosarcoma Phyllodes?
cards.a: Occurs in women > 40 years, mixed fibroepithelial tumor characterized by rapid growth, massive size, stretched skin, and prominent superficial veins; malignant variants metastasize hematogenously rather than via lymphatics.

cards.q: What is the most common causative organism and route of infection in acute lactational mastitis?
cards.a: Staphylococcus aureus; it enters via infant nasopharynx transmission through cracked or fissured nipples into stagnant pools of milk.

cards.q: What are the 3 sequential stages of acute puerperal breast infection and their management?
cards.a:
1. Milk Engorgement: Sectoral fullness/stasis → regular breast evacuation, pumping, warm compresses.
2. Acute Mastitis: Cellulitis (calor, rubor, dolor) → antistaphylococcal antibiotics (e.g., flucloxacillin) and continued feeding/pumping.
3. Acute Abscess: Suppuration/fluctuance/throbbing pain → surgical drainage (I&D or US-guided aspiration) plus antibiotics.

cards.q: What is an antibioma and why is it clinically significant?
cards.a: A sterile, thick-walled chronic pyogenic mass forming when an acute breast abscess is treated with antibiotics without adequate surgical drainage; it forms a hard lump that clinically mimics breast carcinoma.

cards.q: What is the pathophysiology and classic nipple sign of mammary duct ectasia?
cards.a: Dilation of major subareolar lactiferous ducts with debris; periductal chemical irritation and plasma cell infiltration cause chronic scarring and a characteristic slit-like (transverse) nipple retraction.

cards.q: What histological features characterize chronic tuberculous mastitis?
cards.a: Caseating or non-caseating granulomas with epithelioid histiocytes and Langhans giant cells, presenting as cold breast masses or chronically discharging sinus tracts.

cards.q: What does ANDI stand for and what is its primary hormonal etiology?
cards.a: Aberrations of Normal Development and Involution (fibrocystic disease); caused by relative estrogen hyperstimulation unopposed by adequate progesterone.

cards.q: What are the 4 main histopathological components of ANDI (fibrocystic change)?
cards.a:
1. Adenosis (acinar glandular proliferation)
2. Epitheliosis (ductal epithelial hyperplasia)
3. Fibrosis (interlobular stromal hyalinization)
4. Cyst Formation (distended terminal ductules forming 'blue-domed cysts of Bloodgood')

cards.q: What is the classic clinical triad and cyclical pattern of fibrocystic disease (ANDI)?
cards.a:
• Triad: Mastalgia, Nipple Discharge (often green/yellow, non-bloody), and Nodularity (bilateral 'lumpy/cobblestone' texture).
• Pattern: Symptoms worsen premenstrually and regress following menses.

cards.q: What are the 3 components of the standard Triple Assessment Protocol for evaluating breast lesions?
cards.a:
1. Clinical Examination (bilateral breasts, axillae, supraclavicular fossae)
2. Radiological Imaging (Ultrasound if < 35 yrs; Mammography if ≥ 35–40 yrs)
3. Pathological Biopsy (Core needle biopsy [CNB] or fine-needle aspiration cytology [FNAC])
